newsitem.title: INDIA: India politician is detained in corruption scandal.
newsitem.headline: India politician is detained in corruption scandal.

text.p: An Indian politician indicted in a multi-million dollar scandal was on Wednesday detained for a week by a special court as emotional supporters threatened to launch a "fill the jails" protest campaign.

Laloo Prasad Yadav, former chief minister of the poor and populous east Indian state of Bihar, was ordered held in judicial custody by Judge S.K. Lal until August 6 while federal police interrogated him in connection with the $280 million scandal.

Paramilitary police swung out with bamboo staves at angry crowds surrounding the courthouse in the Bihar capital of Patna as hundreds of people lay prostrate or squatted in the street outside to try and block a police convoy carrying Yadav to detention.
The protesters shouted slogans like "We are not afraid of jail or death, we are with Laloo". Many beat their heads on the hoods of the police vehicles.

Yadav, who had ruled Bihar with his unique brand of flamboyant populism for seven years until he was forced to step down last Friday, will be housed in a guest house of the Bihar Military Police converted into a temporary prison by state authorities.

Shyam Rajak and Baidyanath Pandey, ministers in a mammoth 75-member state cabinet now headed by Yadav's unschooled and inexperienced wife Rabri Devi, told Reuters they would launch a "fill the jails" protest campaign across the region.

Judge Lal issued the detention order in his chambers nearly five hours after Yadav surrendered before his court. Under Indian law an accused person can be held in judicial custody for a maximum of two weeks while he is being investigated, and custody can be renewed only if prosecutors present sufficient evidence.

"There is a lot of evidence of conspiracy and involvement of Laloo Yadav in this scam and it was upheld by the High Court also. Since he (Yadav) is very influential he can influence the witnesses and tamper with evidence," a lawyer for the federal Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI) told the judge.

Yadav's detention became inevitable after the Supreme Court on Tuesday rejected his appeal against a Bihar court's refusal to grant him "anticipatory bail", allowed under Indian law to people who apprehend arrest.

Yadav was forced to resign last Friday from leadership of Bihar state after weeks of stubborn resistance following his indictment in April by the CBI in the scandal which involved the siphoning off of state farm funds.
Yadav's exit from power has been clouded by his supporters rubber-stamping his wife Rabri Devi as his successor.
Devi easily won a confidence vote in the state assembly on Monday and has named a mammoth cabinet of 75 ministers.
The crisis in Bihar has drawn widespread criticism because of the central government's helplessness in forcing an indicted politician from power.
Bihar, home to rich coal and iron-ore mines, is the country's second most populous state and one of its poorest.
Only 38 percent of Bihar's population of 93 million can read or write -- the highest illiteracy rate in India. Less than a quarter of its women are literate.

Electoral violence and political corruption are rampant in the state. Clashes between low-caste peasant rights activists and upper-caste landowners, who maintain powerful private armies, are also common. Bad roads make most of Bihar's villages inaccessible to any central legal authority.
